newsitem.title: USA: Chicago mayor proposes $3.77 bln fiscal'97 budget.
newsitem.headline: Chicago mayor proposes $3.77 bln fiscal'97 budget.

text.p: Chicago Mayor Richard Daley proposed a $3.77 billion fiscal 1997 budget Friday that includes $200 million of bonding for various capital improvements.

The budget for the fiscal year that begins Jan. 1 eliminated a projected $67.1 million shortfall that city officials had identified in August. That shortfall projection was the lowest in the city over the last eight years.
On the reey proposed extending a 911 emergency surcharge to cellular phone users to raise about $7 million a year and to change the parking tax system to raise about $5 million a year.
Also proposed for an increase was the city's property tax to support a three-year, $50 million bond-financed program to improve Chicago libraries.
Daley pointed out that an operating property tax hike to support city services was not included in hit.
In his budget address before the Chicago City Council, Daley emphasized that his proposed spending plan would improve neighborhoods.
"Fixing up neighborhoods isn't just good policy, it's good economics. When you pave a street, people build on that street," Daley said. "That's why we have a building boom in our city neighborhoods."

To that end, Daley has proposed a $150 million capital bonding program for fiscal 1997. Under the city's plan, $50 million of the progra funded with proceeds from bonds backed by Chicago-Calumet Skyway revenues.

The plan, announced last week, would be the first new issuance of skyway bonds since the toll bridge connecting the southeast side of Chicago with the northwest corner of Indiana was built in the late 1950s.
It would also be the first new issue since the skyway emerged from a bond default through a current refunding of its outstanding debt in 1994.

Walter Knorr, Chicago's chief financial officer, said the skyway bond plan should come up for final approval by the city at the end of the month. PaineWebber Inc. would be the senior manager for the issue, he said.
The remaining $100 million of Daley's proposed capital bonding plan would be issued as alternate bonds, mainly relying on city sales tax revenues for debt service payments, Knorr said.

He added that no teams have been selected for either the $100 million of alternate bonds or the $50 million of general obligation bonds for city libraries. He said both issues should be voted on by the council sometime in November.
